newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian economy will recover, but after some time.
newsitem.headline: Indian economy will recover, but after some time.

text.p: India's economy, hamstrung by lacklustre industrial growth and sluggish exports, is expected to stage a recovery, but not before late 1997, analysts said on Thursday.
The Commerce Ministry on Wednesday reported that exports -- critical to India's growth -- plunged 10.1 percent in April to $2.52 billion from $2.81 billion in the same month last year.
The unusually large decline, due in part to an 11-day truck strike, compounded concern over the state of the economy.
A survey by a leading industry body on Wednesday showed less than half of India's businessmen expect industrial growth to pick up in the first half of the 1997/98 fiscal year that began on April 1.
Industrial output grew by 7.5 percent in the first 10 months of 1996/97 compared with an 11.7 percent rise in the corresponding period in the previous year.
But economists said they expect growth to pick up in the second half of 1997/98, spurred by increased bank credit, falling interest rates and growth of the agriculture and service sectors.
"We do expect recovery to be slower in the first half," Sanjeev Sanyal, an economist with securities firm Socgen Crosby, told Reuters. "There will be a pick up in the latter half of the year."
The government expects gross domestic product (GDP) to expand by at least seven percent in 1997/98 compared with estimated growth of 6.8 percent in the last fiscal year.
"We expect GDP in 1997/98 to grow at 6.3 percent," Sanyal said. Socgen estimates GDP grew by 6.1 percent in the last fiscal year.
Bidisha Ganguly, an economist with securities firm W.I. Carr, said she expects industrial production to grow by nine percent in 1997/98.
The government's efforts to rein in the fiscal deficit to keep inflation down and spur private investment have put a damper on spending.
India aims to cut the fiscal deficit as a share of GDP to 4.0 percent in 1997/98 from 5.0 percent in the previous year.
"The spending cut has affected demand. There are huge inventories with demand being slack," Sanyal said.
Many sectors like steel, cement, petrochemicals face overcapacity and are carrying large inventories.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) eased credit conditions in April, but the increased flow of funds is taking time to reach industry.
Leading banks cut their prime lending rates by 1-1.5 percentage points to 14.0-14.5 percent after the central bank unveiled its six-monthly monetary policy on April 16.
Abhijit Chakraborti, senior strategist at Lehman Brothers, said interest rates had taken longer than expected to decline.

The prospect of normal monsoon rainfall, predicted by government meteorologists, has boosted the chances of strong agricultural growth. Agriculture is expected to grow by 3.0 percent in 1997/98 compared to 3.7 percent in the previous year, Ganguly said.
The service sector, which accounts for some 40 percent of the economic activity, is projected to grow by about 7.0 percent against 7.4 percent last year, she added.
